subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Close your eyes for a moment. Everything goes dark, doesn't it? Now open them again and look around. In an instant you can see your hands, the room, the colour of the walls, and the bright sky outside the window. Something amazing has just happened, and it happens every single time you open your eyes. That amazing thing is light. In this unit, you are going to become a light detective. You will discover where light comes from, how it travels, why we can see, why shadows appear, and why a mirror can show you your own face.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Explain that we see an object when light bounces off it and travels into our eyes.
Tell the difference between a light source (something that makes its own light) and an object that only reflects light.
Sort light sources into natural ones (like the Sun) and artificial ones (like a torch) that people make.
Explain that light travels in straight lines and use this to explain how shadows form.
Describe how reflection works and why a smooth, shiny surface reflects better than a rough one.
Sort materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by how they let light through.
Explain in simple words how your eye detects light so that you can see.
Follow safety rules that protect your eyes when you work with light.
Here are the important words for this unit. Read each one slowly. You will meet all of them again as you go, so do not worry about memorising them all at once.

concepts.title: We Need Light to See
concepts.explanation:
Let us start with something you have felt many times. Imagine you are in a room at night with no lamp, no torch, and the curtains closed tight. It is completely dark. Can you see the chair? Can you see your own hand in front of your face? No. You cannot see anything at all. Now someone lights a lamp. Suddenly the whole room appears. What changed? Only one thing changed: light. The chair was there the whole time. Your hand was there the whole time. But you could not see them until light was present.

This teaches us the first and most important idea of the whole unit: you cannot see anything in complete darkness. Light must be present for seeing to happen. Some people think their eyes send out a beam that lets them see in the dark, like a cat or an owl. That is not true. Your eyes do not make light. Your eyes can only catch light that is already there. If there is no light, there is nothing for your eyes to catch, and so you see nothing.

Common Misconception: Some children think cats and owls can see in total darkness. They cannot. Their eyes are just very good at catching tiny amounts of light. In complete darkness, with no light at all, even an owl is blind.

This is why you cannot read a book in a pitch-dark room, and why your family lights a lamp or a cooking fire when the Sun goes down. It is also why market traders in Nairobi and Garissa pack up or bring out lanterns when darkness falls. Light comes first, and seeing follows.
concepts.example: Let us think about this a little more, because it is easy to get confused. When you first walk into a dim room, it may seem completely dark, and you cannot see a thing. But wait a few minutes, and slowly you begin to make out the shapes of the furniture. Did the room get brighter? No. Your eyes simply grew better at catching the tiny bit of light that was already there, perhaps a little moonlight sneaking under the door. This is called your eyes adjusting to the dark. It is a helpful trick your eyes can do, but it has a limit. If there is truly no light at all, not even a sliver, then no amount of waiting will help. Your eyes cannot make light out of nothing. This proves once again that seeing always depends on light being present.

concepts.title: Light Sources
concepts.explanation:
If light must be present before we can see, then where does light come from? It comes from a light source. A light source is any object that makes its own light. Think about the objects around you that make their own light. The Sun makes its own light. A candle flame makes its own light. A torch makes its own light. A cooking fire and a firefly make their own light too. These are all light sources.

Now here is a tricky question that catches many people. Is the Moon a light source? At night the Moon looks bright and beautiful over the Indian Ocean. It seems to shine. But the Moon does not make its own light. The Moon is like a giant grey rock in the sky. It only looks bright because sunlight lands on it and bounces off it towards us. So the Moon is not a light source. It is a reflector. This is a very important difference. A light source makes light. A reflector only bounces back light that came from somewhere else.

Did You Know? The Moon looks bright, but it is really a dark, dusty rock. If the Sun switched off, the Moon would vanish into darkness, because it has no light of its own. A firefly, on the other hand, truly makes its own light inside its body. This special glow is called bioluminescence.

We can sort light sources into two groups. Natural light sources are found in nature and are not made by people. The greatest natural light source of all is the Sun. The stars are natural light sources too, though they are so far away they look tiny. Lightning during a coastal storm is a natural light source, and so is a glowing firefly. Even a wild bushfire is a natural source of light.
concepts.example: Artificial light sources are ones that people have made. A torch is artificial. An electric light bulb is artificial. A candle, an oil lamp, a phone screen, and the headlights of a lorry on the road to Berbera are all artificial light sources. People made them. Long ago, before electricity reached many towns, families depended on the Sun by day and on fire, candles, and oil lamps by night. Today many homes use solar panels to catch the strong equatorial sunshine and turn it into electricity for lights after dark. That is a clever way to use a natural source to power an artificial one.

concepts.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
concepts.explanation:
Here is another big idea. Light always travels in straight lines. It does not curve around corners on its own, and it does not bend by itself. Once light leaves a source, it shoots out in perfectly straight lines called rays until it hits something.

You can actually see this. Have you ever seen a beam of sunlight shining through a small gap in a curtain into a dusty room? The dust floating in the air lets you see the beam, and you will notice it is perfectly straight, like a golden rod stretching across the room. In the same way, when you shine a torch in a dark, slightly dusty room, the beam travels in a straight line. Light never wiggles or bends on its own.

How do we know light travels in straight lines even when we cannot see the beam? We know because of shadows. This is one of the best clues in all of science, so read carefully.

A shadow is a dark area that appears when an object blocks the light. Picture a tall acacia tree standing alone on the savanna in the late afternoon. The Sun is low in the sky behind it. On the ground in front of the tree, stretching far away, is a long dark shadow shaped like the tree. Why does that dark shape appear?

The answer is beautiful and simple. Light rays from the Sun travel in straight lines towards the ground. Most of them reach the ground and light it up. But the solid trunk and branches of the tree get in the way of some rays. Because light travels only in straight lines, it cannot bend around the tree to fill in the space behind it. So that space stays dark, and we call the dark shape a shadow. A shadow is really just the place where an object has blocked straight-travelling light.

You can watch shadows change through the day. Early in the morning, when the Sun is low near the horizon, shadows are very long. Your own shadow might stretch far across the ground. At midday, when the strong equatorial Sun is high overhead, shadows become very short, sometimes almost hiding right under your feet. In the late afternoon, as the Sun sinks towards the sea, shadows grow long again. The shadow changes because the direction the light comes from changes as the Sun moves across the sky.
concepts.example: The size of a shadow also depends on how close the object is to the light. If you hold your hand close to a torch, it makes a big shadow on the wall. If you move your hand far from the torch and near the wall, the shadow gets smaller and sharper. Shadow puppets, where you use your hands to make animal shapes on a wall by torchlight, work exactly because of this. You can make a shadow camel, a shadow bird, or a shadow goat.

concepts.title: Reflection and How We See Objects
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to one of the deepest ideas in the whole unit, and it surprises almost everybody. Here is the question: if the Sun and lamps are the only things that make light, then how do you see things that do not make their own light, like a goat, a mango, a book, or your friend's face? None of those objects make light. So how do you see them?

The answer is reflection. Light from a source, such as the Sun, travels in straight lines and lands on the object. The object bounces some of that light off its surface. This bouncing is called reflection. The reflected light then travels in a straight line into your eyes. Only when that reflected light reaches your eyes do you see the object. So seeing a mango works in three steps:

Light leaves a source (for example, the Sun) and travels in a straight line.

The light hits the mango and reflects (bounces) off it.

The reflected light travels into your eyes, and then you see the mango.

This is why you cannot see the mango in a dark room. In the dark there is no light to bounce off it, so no light reaches your eyes, so you see nothing. The mango is still there, but without light there is no reflection, and without reflection there is no seeing. Every single thing you have ever seen that does not glow on its own, you have seen by reflected light. That is a wonderful thought.

Did You Know? When you look at a friend across the room, light has bounced off their face and travelled into your eyes in less than the blink of an eye. You are not really seeing your friend directly. You are seeing the light that reflected off them.

A mirror is a very special reflector. Its surface is extremely smooth and shiny. When light hits a smooth mirror, it bounces off in a neat, even way, so the picture stays clear. That is why you can see your own face in a bathroom mirror. Light from the room bounces off your face, travels to the mirror, bounces off the mirror in an orderly way, and comes back to your eyes. Your face appears in the glass.

You do not need a shop-bought mirror to see reflection. Think about a calm pool of water or a still pond after the rains. When the water is perfectly still and smooth, you can see the sky, the trees, and even your own face reflected in it, almost like a mirror. The still surface of the Indian Ocean on a calm morning can shimmer with reflected sunlight. But what happens when the wind blows and the water becomes rough and choppy? Then the reflection breaks up and disappears. Why?

The reason is about smooth and rough surfaces. A smooth surface, like a mirror or still water, reflects light in an orderly way, so the image stays clear. A rough surface, like choppy water, a brick wall, or a woollen blanket, scatters the light in all different directions. The light still bounces off, which is why you can still see the wall or the blanket, but the light bounces every which way, so you do not see a clear picture in it. This is the key difference: smooth surfaces give clear reflections, and rough surfaces scatter light and give no clear image.

A shiny metal spoon is a fun example. Look at the back of a clean spoon and you see a stretched, curved reflection of your face, because the surface is smooth and shiny, even though it is curved. Look at a rough, dull piece of wood and you see no reflection at all, because the wood scatters the light. Try comparing a shiny spoon, a piece of foil, a sheet of white paper, and a rough cloth. You will find the smoother and shinier something is, the better it reflects.
concepts.example: It is important to understand that a rough surface still reflects light, otherwise you could not see it at all. When you look at a mud-brick wall, a woven mat, or the sandy ground, you are seeing light that has bounced off them into your eyes. The difference is that these rough surfaces scatter the light in every direction, so instead of a clear mirror image you simply see the colour and texture of the surface itself. A mirror is special only because its surface is so smooth that it keeps the bouncing light neat and orderly, so the picture survives the journey to your eyes. Reflection is happening all around you, all the time. Most of it is scattered reflection, and only a few very smooth surfaces give the clear, mirror-like kind.

concepts.title: How Light Passes Through Materials
concepts.explanation:
When light reaches a material, one of a few things can happen. The light might pass straight through, it might pass through in a blurry way, or it might be blocked completely. Because of this, we sort materials into three groups: transparent, translucent, and opaque.

Transparent materials let light pass straight through, so you can see clearly through them. Clean window glass is transparent. A clear plastic bottle is transparent. Clean, still water is transparent, which is why you can see fish swimming in a clear rock pool. When a material is transparent, light travels through it in straight lines and carries a clear picture to your eyes.

Translucent materials let some light through, but they scatter it, so you cannot see a clear picture through them. A thin cotton curtain is translucent. Frosted or misty glass is translucent. Wax paper and a thin plastic bag are translucent too. You can tell there is light on the other side, and you might see blurry shapes and colours, but you cannot see clearly. Translucent things let light through but jumble up the picture.

Opaque materials let no light through at all. Light cannot pass through them, so it is blocked. A wooden door is opaque. A metal pot is opaque. Thick cardboard, a stone wall, a goat-skin mat, and your own body are all opaque. Because opaque objects block light completely, they are the objects that make clear, dark shadows. Remember the acacia tree? A tree trunk is opaque, so it blocks the Sun's light and casts a shadow.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Sunglasses work partly by being translucent. They let some light through so you can still see, but they block a lot of the Sun's strong glare to protect your eyes. A lampshade is often translucent too. It softens a bright bulb into a gentle glow.

concepts.title: Your Amazing Eyes
concepts.explanation:
We keep saying that light enters your eyes so you can see. But what actually happens inside your eye? Let us take a gentle look. Your eye is shaped like a small ball, and it has clever parts that work together to catch light.

At the front of your eye is a clear window called the cornea. Light passes through it first. Behind that is a dark round opening called the pupil. The pupil is the black circle you see in the middle of your eye. It is really a hole that lets light in. The coloured ring around it can make the pupil bigger or smaller to control how much light gets in. In bright equatorial sunshine your pupils shrink to tiny dots to keep out the strong light. In a dim room they open wide to let in as much light as possible. Behind the pupil is the lens, which focuses the light. The light then lands on the retina, a special layer at the back of the eye that detects light. The retina sends a message along the optic nerve to your brain, and your brain works out what you are looking at. Only then do you truly see.

Light reflects off an object and travels to your eye.

It passes through the clear cornea and the pupil.

The lens focuses the light onto the back of the eye.

The retina detects the light and makes a signal.

The optic nerve carries the signal to your brain, and you see.

So seeing is really teamwork between your eyes and your brain. Your eyes catch the light, and your brain turns that light into the pictures you understand. This is why we say vision is the eyes and the brain working together.
concepts.example: Your eyes are wonderfully made, and it is worth taking good care of them. When you read or study, sit where there is enough light so your eyes do not have to strain. Rest your eyes now and then by looking at something far away, like the hills or the horizon over the sea. Eating foods rich in goodness, such as fresh fruit and vegetables, also helps keep your eyes healthy. Your sight is a precious gift, and treating it gently is a wise and thankful thing to do.

methods.title: Can You See in the Dark?
methods.example: To find out whether we can see objects when there is no light at all. Make a Prediction: Before you start, write down what you think. Do you think you will be able to see the objects in a completely dark room? Why or why not?
steps: Place the three objects on a table and look at them in normal light. Note their colours.
With an adult's help, make the room as dark as you safely can. Close curtains and doors.
Wait one minute, then try to see the three objects. Write down exactly what you can and cannot see.
Now switch on the torch and shine it towards the objects (not towards anyone's eyes).
Write down what you can see now.

methods.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
methods.example: To show that light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around corners. Make a Prediction: If you make three cards with a hole in each, do you think you will see the torch only when all three holes line up in a straight line?
steps: Make a small hole in the centre of each card, all at the same height.
Stand the three cards in a row on a table, one behind the other, so the holes line up in a straight line.
In a dim room, shine the torch through the first hole. Look through the last card. Can you see the light?
Now slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer in line with the others.
Shine the torch again and look. Can you still see the light through the holes?

methods.title: Making and Changing Shadows
methods.example: To investigate how the size of a shadow changes when you move an object closer to or further from a light. Make a Prediction: What do you think happens to a shadow when you move the object closer to the torch? Does it get bigger or smaller?
steps: In a dim room, hold the torch still and shine it at the wall.
Hold the object halfway between the torch and the wall so it makes a shadow on the wall.
Measure the height of the shadow and write it down.
Move the object closer to the torch. Measure the shadow again.
Move the object closer to the wall. Measure the shadow again.

methods.title: Smooth and Rough Reflectors
methods.example: To find out which surfaces reflect light best and give the clearest picture. Make a Prediction: Which do you think will give the clearest reflection: a mirror, a shiny spoon, kitchen foil, white paper, or a rough cloth? Put them in order before you start.
steps: In a dim room, hold each item up one at a time and try to see your face or the room in it.
Shine the torch gently onto each surface (never towards eyes) and watch how the light bounces.
Give each surface a score from 1 (no clear reflection) to 5 (very clear reflection).
Now compare the smooth foil with the crumpled foil.

methods.title: Transparent, Translucent, or Opaque?
methods.example: To sort materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by testing how light passes through them. Make a Prediction: Look at your materials and predict which will be transparent (clear), translucent (blurry), and opaque (blocks light).
steps: In a dim room, hold each material in front of the torch, one at a time.
Shine the torch through the material towards a wall (not towards eyes).
Decide: does all the light pass through (transparent), some blurry light (translucent), or no light (opaque)?
Try to see a shape or your fingers through each material.

workedExamples.title: Measuring a Shadow
workedExamples.prompt: Some light questions involve simple measuring. Let us work through one together, step by step. Amina wants to find out how the shadow of a stick changes as the Sun moves. She pushes a straight stick into the ground and measures the length of its shadow at three times of day.
workedExamples.solution:
She writes down her results:

Shadow length

Where the Sun is

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: We can see objects that do not make their own light because: (a) our eyes send out beams; (b) light reflects off them into our eyes; (c) the objects glow; (d) our brain imagines them.
workedExamples.solution: 1: (b) Light reflects off objects into our eyes. Our eyes do not send out beams; they catch light.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a natural light source? (a) a torch; (b) an electric bulb; (c) the Sun; (d) a mirror.
workedExamples.solution: 2: (c) The Sun is natural. Torches and bulbs are made by people, so they are artificial. A mirror is not a source at all.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a light source? (a) the Moon; (b) a mirror; (c) a candle flame; (d) a white wall.
workedExamples.solution: 3: (c) A candle flame makes its own light. The Moon, a mirror, and a white wall only reflect light.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Light travels in: (a) curved paths; (b) straight lines; (c) circles; (d) zig-zags on its own.
workedExamples.solution: 4: (b) Light travels in straight lines. This is why shadows form.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: A shadow forms because an object: (a) makes darkness; (b) blocks light that travels in straight lines; (c) absorbs the Sun; (d) reflects light.
workedExamples.solution: 5: (b) A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks straight-travelling light, so a dark area is left behind it.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which surface gives the clearest reflection? (a) rough cloth; (b) a smooth mirror; (c) crumpled foil; (d) dry sand.
workedExamples.solution: 6: (b) A smooth mirror reflects light in an orderly way and gives the clearest image. Rough surfaces scatter light.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A material you can see through clearly is called: (a) opaque; (b) translucent; (c) transparent; (d) reflective.
workedExamples.solution: 7: (c) Transparent materials let light through clearly so you can see through them.

activities.title: Can You See in the Dark?
activities.materials: A small room you can make very dark (a room with thick curtains, or a large cupboard with an adult's permission); Three small objects of different colours, such as a red cup, a spoon, and a cloth; A torch
steps: Place the three objects on a table and look at them in normal light. Note their colours.
With an adult's help, make the room as dark as you safely can. Close curtains and doors.
Wait one minute, then try to see the three objects. Write down exactly what you can and cannot see.
Now switch on the torch and shine it towards the objects (not towards anyone's eyes).
Write down what you can see now.
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers.

activities.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
activities.materials: Three pieces of card or stiff paper of the same size; A pencil and a small coin to draw and cut equal holes (ask an adult to help with cutting); Some lumps of clay, dough, or tape to stand the cards up; A torch
steps: Make a small hole in the centre of each card, all at the same height.
Stand the three cards in a row on a table, one behind the other, so the holes line up in a straight line.
In a dim room, shine the torch through the first hole. Look through the last card. Can you see the light?
Now slide the middle card sideways so its hole is no longer in line with the others.
Shine the torch again and look. Can you still see the light through the holes?
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers.

activities.title: Making and Changing Shadows
activities.materials: A torch; A small opaque object, such as a plastic toy, a spoon, or a small cup; A light-coloured wall or a sheet of white paper taped to a wall; A ruler or measuring tape
steps: In a dim room, hold the torch still and shine it at the wall.
Hold the object halfway between the torch and the wall so it makes a shadow on the wall.
Measure the height of the shadow and write it down.
Move the object closer to the torch. Measure the shadow again.
Move the object closer to the wall. Measure the shadow again.

activities.title: Smooth and Rough Reflectors
activities.materials: A mirror (ask an adult if it is glass); A clean, shiny metal spoon; A piece of smooth kitchen foil and a piece of crumpled foil; A sheet of white paper; A rough cloth or piece of cardboard; A torch
steps: In a dim room, hold each item up one at a time and try to see your face or the room in it.
Shine the torch gently onto each surface (never towards eyes) and watch how the light bounces.
Give each surface a score from 1 (no clear reflection) to 5 (very clear reflection).
Now compare the smooth foil with the crumpled foil.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Transparent, Translucent, or Opaque?
activities.materials: A torch; Clear plastic or a clean clear bottle; A thin cloth or thin paper; Wax paper or a thin plastic bag; Cardboard, wood, or a metal lid; A cup of clean water
steps: In a dim room, hold each material in front of the torch, one at a time.
Shine the torch through the material towards a wall (not towards eyes).
Decide: does all the light pass through (transparent), some blurry light (translucent), or no light (opaque)?
Try to see a shape or your fingers through each material.
Safety: Plastic bags are not toys — never put them over or near your face.

activities.title: Observe: Your Amazing Eyes
activities.materials: A small room you can make very dark (a room with thick curtains, or a large cupboard with an adult's permission); Three small objects of different colours, such as a red cup, a spoon, and a cloth; A torch
steps: Look for an example of your amazing eyes around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Group and Transparent.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Shadows Prove Light Travels Straight
rules.text: A shadow forms on the OPPOSITE side of an object from the light source. If light could bend around objects, shadows would be impossible. Shadows are proof that light travels in straight lines.

rules.title: Why Some Surfaces Make Images
rules.text: Smooth and shiny surfaces (mirror, still water, polished metal) reflect light in an orderly way and make a clear image. Rough or dull surfaces (a wall, cloth, choppy water, sand) scatter light in all directions and make no clear image.

connections.text: Light is a form of energy, like heat and electricity. Solar panels change light energy into electrical energy.
Plants need sunlight to grow, and our eyes let us see the world around us.
Measuring shadow lengths and reflection uses rulers, tables, and comparing numbers.
The strong equatorial Sun, the seasons, and day and night all connect to light.
Artists use light, shadow, and reflection to make pictures look real.
Watch how your shadow changes from morning to evening and keep a simple diary.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why you cannot see anything in a completely dark room.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 1. In complete darkness there is no light to reflect off objects into your eyes, so you see nothing. Objects are still there, but without light there is no seeing.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is the difference between a light source and a reflector? Give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 2. A light source makes its own light (for example, the Sun or a torch). A reflector only bounces back light that came from somewhere else (for example, the Moon or a mirror).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, in three steps, how you are able to see a goat standing in a field.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3. Step 1: light from a source (like the Sun) travels to the goat. Step 2: the light reflects off the goat. Step 3: the reflected light enters your eyes, so you see the goat.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why does an opaque object make a shadow?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 4. An opaque object does not let light through, so it blocks the straight-travelling light. The space behind it stays dark, and that dark area is the shadow.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why can you see your face clearly in still water but not in choppy water?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5. Still water is smooth, so it reflects light in an orderly way and gives a clear image. Choppy water is rough, so it scatters the light in all directions and the picture breaks up.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the three groups we sort materials into by how they let light through, and give one example of each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 6. Transparent (clear glass, water), translucent (thin curtain, frosted glass), and opaque (wood, metal).

rounds.prompt: A material you can see through clearly is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Transparent materials let light through clearly so you can see through them.

rounds.prompt: Your shadow is longest when the Sun is:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: When the Sun is low near the horizon, light comes in at a slant and shadows are long.

rounds.prompt: We can see objects that do not make their own light because:
choices: light reflects off them into our eyes;
rounds.answer: light reflects off them into our eyes;
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Light reflects off objects into our eyes. Our eyes do not send out beams; they catch light.

rounds.prompt: Light travels in:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Light travels in straight lines. This is why shadows form.

games.title: Explain It: Shadow
games.description: Practise shadow through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Frosted glass and a thin curtain are examples of:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it, so the view is blurry.

rounds.prompt: The Moon looks bright at night because it:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: The Moon reflects sunlight; it does not make its own light.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a natural light source?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: The Sun is natural. Torches and bulbs are made by people, so they are artificial. A mirror is not a source at all.

rounds.prompt: A shadow forms because an object:
choices: blocks light that travels in straight lines;
rounds.answer: blocks light that travels in straight lines;
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks straight-travelling light, so a dark area is left behind it.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Transparent
games.description: Practise transparent through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: The part of the eye that detects light at the back is the:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: The retina at the back of the eye detects light and sends a signal to the brain.

rounds.prompt: Which is the correct safety rule?
choices: stare at the Sun to test your eyes;
never look directly at the Sun;
rounds.answer: never look directly at the Sun;
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Never look directly at the Sun, because it can permanently damage your eyes.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a light source?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A candle flame makes its own light. The Moon, a mirror, and a white wall only reflect light.

rounds.prompt: Which surface gives the clearest reflection?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 5 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A smooth mirror reflects light in an orderly way and gives the clearest image. Rough surfaces scatter light.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can explain that we see an object when light bounces off it and travels into our eyes.
I can tell the difference between a light source (something that makes its own light) and an object that only reflects light.
I can sort light sources into natural ones (like the Sun) and artificial ones (like a torch) that people make.
I can explain that light travels in straight lines and use this to explain how shadows form.
I can describe how reflection works and why a smooth, shiny surface reflects better than a rough one.
I can sort materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by how they let light through.
I can explain in simple words how your eye detects light so that you can see.
